items.why_watch: Max Miller digs into the disputed history of who actually invented the piña colada — a question with more legitimate competing claims than you'd expect. At 14 minutes, it's a tight deep-dive that treats a cocktail origin story with the same rigor usually reserved for more "serious" history. You'll finish with a recipe and a new go-to party fact.

items.why_watch: Three compact History Guy profiles of genuine American oddballs: a man who declared himself Emperor of the United States, a merchant whose spectacular bad luck somehow reversed into fortune, and a congressman who showed up to Capitol Hill channeling Jesus. Each story is self-contained and strange enough to feel invented, which is precisely why they're worth 46 minutes.

items.why_watch: Oxford mathematician Alain Goriely traces knot theory from Lord Kelvin's 19th-century atomic theory (knots as building blocks of matter — wrong, but productive) through to modern applications in DNA biology and solar physics. At nearly an hour, this is a proper Gresham College lecture, so come ready to think — but the payoff is a genuine sense of how a purely abstract mathematical field quietly explains the physical world.

items.why_watch: Terence Tao — arguably the greatest living mathematician — walks through six foundational mathematical concepts in a single sitting, which is a rare chance to hear someone at the absolute frontier of the field explain basics with total clarity and no condescension. The 84-minute runtime earns its length: Tao's explanations consistently illuminate *why* these concepts matter, not just what they are.
